options.name: LiveKit (self-hosted)
options.license: Apache-2.0 (server, all client SDKs, and the React component library). No open-core/BSL catch found: the self-hosted server is the same SFU the Cloud runs. Note some third-party blogs wrongly call it MIT — the GitHub API reports Apache-2.0.
options.maintained: Very actively. Last push to livekit/livekit 7 Sep 2026 (i.e. today); client-sdk-js 3 Sep 2026; components-js 2 Sep 2026. @livekit/components-react on npm at 2.9.24, Apache-2.0, peer dep React >=18 (so React 19 is fine).
options.whatItDoes: A Go SFU (selective forwarding unit) plus signalling, room/participant model, JWT-based access tokens with per-room grants, simulcast, adaptive stream and dynacast (server drops layers nobody is watching), plus optional egress/ingress. Ships a browser SDK (livekit-client) and an official React component library. It is the one option in this lane that bundles SFU + signalling + TURN + a React SDK in a single deployable binary.
options.serverNeeded: One `livekit-server` binary/container. Single-node needs NO Redis (Redis only for multi-node state). Official multi-arch Docker images including linux/arm64, ~31 MB compressed — this matters, it will run natively on the Oracle Ampere box. Ports: 443 (HTTPS/TURN-TLS), 80 (cert issuance), 7881/TCP (WebRTC over TCP fallback), 3478/UDP (TURN/UDP), 50000-60000/UDP (media). Docs' reference deploy is Docker Compose + Caddy with automatic Let's Encrypt/ZeroSSL certs. Crucially it has an EMBEDDED TURN/STUN server, so no separate coturn is required. Docs do not publish RAM/CPU figures; community/deployment guides converge on 2 vCPU / 2-4 GB for small deployments, with the server process itself typically under 1 GB RSS. Treat those as community numbers, not vendor-stated.
options.fitsUs: Best structural fit of anything I checked. Static Vercel SPA connects over WebSocket + WebRTC to your own host — no Node server in front of the SPA needed. The one server-side piece is minting an access token, and that is a ~20-line Supabase Deno edge function signing a JWT with the LiveKit API secret; it can read the caller's Supabase JWT and encode role (parent/child/guest) into the room grants, which is exactly the role-aware, privacy-first model the brief demands (a child can be issued a token with canPublish/canSubscribe scoped, or simply not issued a token for a room at all). CSP additions are one wss:// origin and one https:// origin for your own host. @livekit/components-react gives working primitives, but do NOT ship its default conference UI — it reads corporate. Use the hooks (useParticipants, useTracks, useRoomContext) and build the warm five-year-old-friendly surface yourself; the hooks-not-components path is well documented.
options.cost: Self-hosted: £0 in licence. Compute = the Oracle VM you already have (or a second Always Free Ampere instance). Bandwidth = Oracle Always Free includes 10 TB/month egress, which is enormous relative to family calling — a 4-way 30-minute call relayed through the SFU is on the order of a few hundred MB of egress, so thousands of family-hours/month sit inside the free allowance. LiveKit CLOUD, by contrast, is exactly the trap the brief warns about: the free 'Build' tier is 5,000 WebRTC minutes, 50 GB downstream, 100 concurrent connections; the next step is 'Ship' at $50/mo (150,000 WebRTC minutes, 250 GB then $0.12/GB) and 'Scale' at $500/mo. WebRTC minutes are per-participant-minute, so a 5-person 40-minute family call burns 200 minutes. Free tier ≈ 25 such calls a month across the entire product. Do not build the business on LiveKit Cloud.
options.risks: Real, and I want to be blunt about them: (1) It is a new always-on service with a wide UDP port range, a public IP, DNS and TLS to keep alive — a genuine new failure mode, and one that fails in the worst way (silently, only for some users, only on some networks). (2) It would share the small arm64 box with Pipecat and worker-cron; media forwarding is CPU-bound and Pipecat is already CPU-hungry. I'd put LiveKit on its own Always Free Ampere instance rather than co-tenant it. (3) You now operate a TURN relay: 15-20% of consumer WebRTC sessions cannot connect peer-to-peer and must relay, and that fraction is materially higher on Nigerian mobile carriers with symmetric CGNAT — so Mama Fọláké is disproportionately likely to be a relayed session, and YOU pay that bandwidth. Inside Oracle's 10 TB it is free; it is not free of responsibility. (4) There is an open memory-leak issue thread (livekit/livekit#3614) — I did not read it in depth and cannot say whether current versions are affected; verify before production. (5) Bus factor is fine (VC-backed company, large contributor base) but the company's centre of gravity has visibly shifted to AI voice agents ('End-to-end realtime stack for connecting humans and AI'), so plain human-to-human video is no longer the headline use case.

options.name: Jitsi Meet (self-hosted)
options.license: Apache-2.0 (jitsi-meet, lib-jitsi-meet, and jitsi-meet-react-sdk all Apache-2.0)
options.stars: ~29,900 — the most-starred option here. jitsi-meet-react-sdk is only ~77 stars.
options.maintained: Yes, very actively: last push 6 Sep 2026. But note the maintenance is concentrated on the flagship app; the React SDK is a thinner, less-loved wrapper (last push 13 Aug 2026, 19 open issues, 77 stars).
options.whatItDoes: A complete, batteries-included conferencing product: web app, mobile apps, JVB (Jitsi Videobridge, the SFU), Prosody (XMPP signalling), Jicofo (conference focus), optional Jibri (recording) and Jigasi (SIP). Notably it does true P2P for exactly 2 participants (`p2p: { enabled: true }`) and transparently promotes to the JVB when a third joins — a genuinely useful property for a family app whose commonest call is a 1:1 with grandma.
options.serverNeeded: The heaviest stack in this lane. JVB + Prosody + Jicofo + nginx, each a separate process, typically via docker-jitsi-meet. Requires 10000/UDP open for media. Community guidance: 2 cores / 4 GB dedicated as a floor, 8 GB commonly recommended; ~1 GB idle rising to 2-4 GB in active meetings. That is a lot of always-on footprint for calls that will usually have two people in them. Also needs coturn separately for reliable relay in restrictive networks.
options.fitsUs: Two embedding paths, both compromised for us. (a) The IFrame API / @jitsi/react-sdk drops Jitsi's own entire UI into an iframe. It works in a static SPA in an afternoon, but you inherit a corporate conferencing UI you cannot meaningfully reshape — directly against 'warm rather than corporate', and hopeless for a five-year-old. Theming is limited to config flags and CSS overrides you don't control inside the frame. (b) lib-jitsi-meet is the low-level library that lets you build your own UI on Jitsi's signalling — full control, but it is XMPP-based, thinly documented relative to LiveKit, and you are writing against an API primarily maintained for Jitsi's own client. Role-awareness maps awkwardly: Jitsi's model is moderator/participant with JWT auth, not the parent/child/guest gradient we need, so guest scoping would be bolted on.
options.cost: Self-hosted: £0 licence, but the highest infrastructure cost in this lane — realistically its own 4 GB+ VM, which the Oracle Always Free Ampere allocation can cover but which will not comfortably co-tenant with Pipecat.
options.risks: Operationally the most to go wrong: four interacting services, XMPP in the middle, and a well-earned reputation for upgrades breaking working installs. The docs themselves warn that misconfiguration destroys basic functionality rather than merely slowing it. And the strategic risk: Jitsi is 8x8's open-source funnel into a paid SaaS, so the incentive to keep self-hosting frictionless is structurally weak.

options.name: Jitsi hosted — meet.jit.si and 8x8 JaaS
options.license: Software Apache-2.0, but the HOSTED SERVICE is governed by 8x8's terms, not the licence — this distinction is the whole point of this row.
options.maintained: Service actively operated by 8x8.
options.whatItDoes: Free public instance at meet.jit.si, and the commercial 'Jitsi as a Service' (JaaS) API product.
options.serverNeeded: None — that is the appeal, and the bait.
options.fitsUs: Technically it embeds in the SPA in an hour via @jitsi/react-sdk. Commercially it does not fit, and I'd class relying on meet.jit.si as not legitimate for a product sold to families.
options.cost: meet.jit.si terms cap free use at 25 active endpoints per calendar month across all your accounts, and 8x8 reserves the right to throttle you or force you onto a paid plan above that. If you embed it in a commercial product for third parties you must also let 8x8 branding remain visible for at least 15 seconds, unaltered — i.e. your family app shows another company's logo to Mama Fọláké. JaaS proper: free to 25 MAU (an MAU = a unique user who attended at least one meeting with at least one other user that month), then $99/mo to 300 MAU, $499 to 1,500, $999 to 3,000, with $0.99 per MAU overage. A family is ~5-7 MAU, so 300 MAU ≈ 45 families for $99/mo. That is a per-user SaaS bill scaling linearly with the exact thing you are selling.
options.risks: Disqualifying on three counts: the 25-endpoint/25-MAU free ceiling is reached by roughly four demo families; the pricing scales per-family; and the branding requirement puts 8x8's identity inside a product whose entire premise is intimate family space. Also every call would traverse a third party you have no data agreement with, against 'privacy-first'. Use meet.jit.si for a throwaway prototype if you like — never for the shipped product.

options.name: mediasoup
options.maintained: Yes, actively — last push 6 Sep 2026.
options.whatItDoes: A high-quality SFU engine: C++ worker subprocesses doing ICE/DTLS/RTP, driven by a Node.js (or Rust) control library. Excellent congestion control and codec handling; widely respected as the best-engineered SFU core in the open-source world.
options.serverNeeded: Its own documentation is explicit that it is 'not a standalone server but an unopinionated Node.js module'. You must build, yourself: the signalling layer, room/session management, authentication and authorisation, reconnection logic, and the client application. Plus a Node.js runtime always-on, plus native C++ workers to compile for arm64, plus coturn separately (no built-in TURN).
options.fitsUs: Poorly, and this is the clearest 'no' in the list for our constraints. The brief says 'No Node server of our own in front of it' — mediasoup requires exactly that, and not a trivial one: a stateful, always-on Node signalling server holding room state, which then also needs its own scaling and failure story. Everything LiveKit gives you free (tokens, room model, React SDK, TURN) is homework here.
options.cost: £0 licence; the cost is engineering weeks and a second always-on stateful service.
options.risks: Not a maintenance risk — a scope risk. Choosing mediasoup means committing to build and then operate a bespoke conferencing backend. For a family-calling feature inside a larger product, that is disproportionate. Reasonable choice only if you needed media control nobody else offers; we don't.

options.name: Janus Gateway
options.license: GPL-3.0 — the licence deserves attention. The server is GPLv3; Meetecho sell commercial licences. Since we would run it as a network service and not distribute it, GPLv3 (not AGPL) does not force us to publish our app, but it is still the most restrictive licence in this lane and worth a legal glance before committing.
options.maintained: Yes — last push 4 Sep 2026. Long-standing, credible maintainer (Meetecho).
options.whatItDoes: A general-purpose WebRTC server in C, built as a set of plugins (VideoRoom for SFU conferencing, AudioBridge for mixed audio, plus streaming/SIP/recording). Very mature and battle-tested, particularly in broadcast and telecom contexts.
options.serverNeeded: A C daemon plus configuration per plugin, a signalling transport (its own WebSocket/HTTP API), and coturn separately. You still write your own room, auth and UI layer against the VideoRoom plugin's API. Compiles on arm64 but you are managing a C build/dependency chain rather than pulling one static binary.
options.fitsUs: Workable but unrewarding. There is no official React SDK; you'd use janus.js (a fairly dated, callback-style JS library) or a community wrapper, and hand-roll auth. Its AudioBridge plugin is genuinely interesting for us — server-side audio MIXING means a participant on a poor Nigerian mobile connection receives ONE mixed audio stream instead of N, which is the single most bandwidth-friendly way to do a family voice call. That is a real, specific advantage worth remembering even if we don't pick Janus.
options.cost: £0 licence (GPLv3), self-hosted infrastructure only.
options.risks: GPLv3 needs a deliberate decision rather than a shrug. The client story is dated relative to LiveKit. Configuration surface is large and plugin-specific. Fine engineering, wrong ergonomics for a small team shipping a family app.

options.name: ion-sfu
options.maintained: NO — do not use. Last push 21 July 2023, over three years ago. The repository is not formally archived, which makes it look alive to a casual glance; it is not. The wider ion project has been dormant for a comparable period.
options.whatItDoes: A pure-Go SFU built on Pion, originally an attractive lightweight alternative to Janus/mediasoup.
options.serverNeeded: Go binary + your own signalling + coturn.
options.fitsUs: It would have fitted the arm64 box nicely. That is now irrelevant.
options.cost: £0, and worth exactly that.
options.risks: Unmaintained for 3+ years means unpatched WebRTC/Pion security fixes, no browser-compatibility tracking (Chrome and Safari have shipped multiple WebRTC behaviour changes since 2023), and no recourse when it breaks. Flagging explicitly because it still appears in 'best open-source SFU' listicles and would be an easy mistake to make. Exclude.

options.name: Galène
options.maintained: Yes, and genuinely so — last push 6 Sep 2026, latest tag galene-1.2. Development is funded by NLnet's NGI0Core programme and has had recent security audits. It has no GitHub 'releases', only tags, so automated freshness checks can misleadingly 404.
options.whatItDoes: A deliberately minimal, low-resource videoconference server in Go, written for university teaching and used in production at French universities. Server-side selective forwarding with a documented, stable client protocol.
options.serverNeeded: The lightest real SFU here by a distance: ONE static Go binary (`CGO_ENABLED=0 go build`), NO database (JSON config files in data/), and a BUILT-IN TURN server. Ports: 8443/TCP for HTTP(S), 1194 TCP+UDP for TURN, plus a restrictable high UDP range for media. Its own figures: ~300 one-to-one participants per CPU core; roughly 20 participants per core for active many-to-many video; a 100-student lecture on about a quarter of a core. A six-person family call is a rounding error on the Oracle box — it could genuinely co-tenant with Pipecat, which nothing else here can.
options.fitsUs: Surprisingly well on infrastructure, less well on client ergonomics. There is a documented protocol (galene-protocol.md) and a JS/TS client library plus a 'writing clients' guide (galene-client.md), so a custom React UI is a supported path, not a hack — and since we must build a warm bespoke UI anyway, having no default conference UI to fight is arguably a feature. But there are no React bindings, no hooks, no component library: you write the WebSocket protocol handling and track plumbing yourself. Its auth model is groups + users managed via `galenectl`, which does not map cleanly onto Supabase identities and RLS; wiring parent/child/guest to it would be custom work.
options.cost: £0 licence, and the lowest infrastructure cost of any SFU here.
options.risks: Be honest about two things. (1) Bus factor: this is essentially one maintainer (Juliusz Chroboczek) plus grant funding. Excellent code, genuine longevity so far, but if he stops, we own a Go SFU. (2) The built-in TURN is IPv4-only and defaults to port 1194 rather than TLS on 443 — restrictive corporate/mobile networks that only permit 443 will fail where LiveKit's TURN-over-TLS-on-443 succeeds, and that is precisely the Nigerian-mobile scenario we cannot afford to lose. Mitigable by fronting it with coturn on 443, but then the 'one binary' simplicity is gone. Also no end-to-end encryption — the operator can in principle see media, which we must not overstate in privacy copy.

options.name: Plain WebRTC mesh + self-hosted coturn (no SFU at all)
options.license: coturn: BSD-3-Clause style (GitHub reports NOASSERTION because the file bundles several notices; it is permissive and is the de facto standard TURN server). Browser WebRTC itself needs no licence.
options.maintained: coturn: actively — last push 6 Sep 2026. It is the reference TURN implementation and is packaged for Debian/Ubuntu arm64.
options.whatItDoes: No media server at all. Browsers connect directly to each other; each participant sends their stream to every other participant. Signalling (offer/answer/ICE candidate exchange) rides on a channel you already own. coturn exists only to relay the minority of connections that cannot go direct.
options.serverNeeded: Only coturn — a small, stable, well-understood daemon, tens of MB of RAM, effectively no CPU (it shuffles packets), on ports 3478 and 5349/443 for TURN-over-TLS. No SFU, no signalling server: Supabase Realtime broadcast channels carry SDP and ICE candidates, which is exactly what they are for, and Supabase Postgres+RLS carries call invitations and state. This is the only option that adds NO new always-on service you have to reason about beyond a relay that is dormant most of the time.
options.fitsUs: For the actual demo scenario — Ifeoluwa on a video call with Mama Fọláké at 14:00 — it fits perfectly and beats every SFU on latency, because the media never touches a server at all when a direct path exists. Role-awareness and privacy live entirely in Postgres RLS, where the rest of the product's policy already lives, rather than being duplicated into a second system's auth model. Chat is just a table + Realtime. CSP addition is one turn:/turns: origin.
options.cost: Effectively £0. coturn on the existing Oracle VM; relay bandwidth is billed as Oracle egress against a 10 TB/month Always Free allowance. Be honest about who pays: WE pay the relay bandwidth, for the ~15-20% of sessions that need it — and the true rate will be higher than 15-20% for the Nigeria leg, because carrier-grade symmetric NAT is the classic TURN-forcing case. Even so, a relayed 1:1 video call is roughly 0.5-1 Mbps each way; an hour is well under a gigabyte. Thousands of hours fit inside the free allowance.
options.risks: One hard ceiling, and it is the reason this cannot be the whole answer: mesh does not scale. Each participant uploads N-1 copies of their stream. At 2 it is ideal. At 3 it is fine. At 4-5 it is the widely-cited practical limit and already punishing on mobile — 4 participants at 1 Mbps means 3 Mbps sustained upload each, which a Nigerian mobile uplink will often not sustain, and mesh video will flatten a mid-range Android battery inside an hour. At 8 it is simply broken: 7 encodes and 7 uploads per device. Since the Adeyemis plus two guests is SEVEN people, a whole-family call is outside mesh's range by design. Also: no server-side recording, and no way to drop layers for a weak participant.

recommendation:
Self-host LiveKit on its own Oracle Always Free Ampere instance, mint access tokens from a Supabase edge function, and build the UI yourself on @livekit/components-react's HOOKS rather than its default conference components.

The reasoning, in order of what actually decides it:

1. It is the only option that collapses SFU + signalling + TURN + a maintained React SDK into ONE arm64 binary. Every alternative leaves us assembling two or three of those ourselves — mediasoup needs a bespoke Node signalling server (explicitly against our constraints), Janus and Galène need custom client and auth layers, Jitsi needs four interacting services.

2. The token model fits our privacy spine exactly. A Supabase edge function reads the caller's Supabase JWT, checks the same RLS-backed family/role tables the rest of Wàfè uses, and mints a LiveKit token whose grants encode parent/child/guest. A child is not kept out of a call by UI — they are never issued a token. "A child never sees something simply because they belong to the family" becomes an enforced server-side property, not a front-end promise.

3. Self-hosting sidesteps the two commercial traps in this space. LiveKit Cloud's free tier (5,000 WebRTC participant-minutes) is about 25 family calls a month across the entire product; 8x8's JaaS is $99/mo for roughly 45 families AND requires their branding inside our app. Both scale per-family, which is fatal for a marketplace product. The Apache-2.0 self-hosted server has no such ceiling and no open-core catch.

4. Bandwidth honesty: we pay for TURN relay, and the Nigeria leg will relay more often than the 15-20% consumer baseline because carrier NAT is the classic forcing case. But LiveKit's embedded TURN does TLS on 443, which is what actually gets through restrictive mobile networks, and Oracle's Always Free 10 TB/month egress swallows thousands of family-call hours. This is affordable — but it is an operational responsibility, not free magic.

5. It scales through the whole realistic range. At 2 participants an SFU adds one hop of latency versus mesh — a real but small cost. At 5 it is comfortable. At 8 (the Adeyemis plus both guests) it still works, where a mesh is simply broken. Picking LiveKit means not building the calling feature twice.

Two dissenting notes I want on the record rather than buried:

- If the appetite for a new always-on service is genuinely zero, the honest minimal answer is mesh WebRTC signalled over Supabase Realtime broadcast plus a coturn relay. For the literal demo scenario — one grandmother, one video call — it is better than LiveKit: lower latency, no media server, no new stateful component. It dies at 5+ participants. Ship it only if you accept that a whole-family call is out of scope, and know you will rebuild on an SFU later.

- Galène is the one I would keep in the back pocket. Single MIT Go binary, no database, built-in TURN, ~20 participants per core, light enough to co-tenant with Pipecat. If the LiveKit deployment proves too heavy for the infrastructure we are willing to run, Galène is the credible fallback — with the caveats that its TURN is IPv4-only on port 1194 (weaker than LiveKit's TLS-on-443 exactly where we need it most) and that it is essentially a one-maintainer project.

Whichever we choose: build CHAT on Supabase Postgres + RLS + Realtime, not on any of these. Every option here is media infrastructure; none of them should own our messages, and putting chat in Postgres keeps the role-aware privacy rules in one place.
notes:
Verification method: I hit the GitHub API directly for licence/stars/pushed_at rather than trusting listicles, and read the projects' own docs for requirements. Everything below is where I am NOT confident.

Explicitly excluded after checking: ion-sfu (last push 21 July 2023 — three years dead, and dangerously it is NOT archived so it still reads as alive; unpatched Pion, no tracking of Chrome/Safari WebRTC changes since 2023). Owncast was correctly excluded by the brief — it is one-to-many live streaming with no return path, structurally incapable of a two-way call.

Where I am unsure and did not guess:
- LiveKit publishes no official RAM/CPU requirements. The "2 vCPU / 2-4 GB, under 1 GB RSS" figures are from community deployment guides, not the vendor. Load-test before trusting them.
- There is an open memory-leak issue (livekit/livekit#3614). I saw the title in search results and did NOT read the thread. Someone should, before production.
- I do not know the actual shape of your existing Oracle VM (OCPU count, RAM, whether it is inside the 4-OCPU/24 GB Ampere Always Free allocation or a separate paid shape). My "give LiveKit its own instance" advice assumes headroom exists in the Always Free allocation; if the current box IS the whole allocation, this becomes a real cost decision rather than a free one. Worth confirming before planning.
- Oracle's 10 TB/month free egress is well attested across multiple sources but I verified it via search summaries, not Oracle's own pricing page. Confirm on Oracle's site before relying on it as the budget argument — it is load-bearing for my recommendation.
- I did not verify LiveKit's arm64 image by pulling it; "multi-arch, ~31 MB compressed" comes from Docker Hub tag listings surfaced in search. Cheap to confirm: `docker manifest inspect livekit/livekit-server:latest`.
- The meet.jit.si "25 active endpoints per calendar month" figure comes from my read of 8x8's terms page. The 15-second branding requirement and the throttle-or-upgrade clause I am confident about; the exact endpoint number should be re-read from the terms directly if anyone is tempted by that path.
- I did not evaluate end-to-end encryption in any depth. LiveKit supports insertable-streams E2EE; Galène explicitly does NOT (its docs say the operator could in principle access the media); Jitsi has E2EE with caveats. For a product marketed as privacy-first this deserves its own investigation, because the marketing copy we write is constrained by what is actually true here — and "the family's calls are private" means something different if our own server can see them.

Outside my lane but flagged because it bears on the decision: managed WebRTC from Cloudflare (Realtime/Calls) is the obvious non-self-hosted comparator with different economics from LiveKit Cloud and JaaS. I did not investigate it — presumably another agent's lane — but the recommendation above should be sanity-checked against it before anyone builds.

Two things that came up which I think are more valuable than the vendor comparison itself:

First, Jitsi's automatic P2P-for-exactly-two behaviour is the right IDEA regardless of vendor. The commonest call in this product is a 1:1 with grandma, and routing that through an SFU adds a hop for no benefit. LiveKit does not do this automatically. Worth considering a deliberate hybrid later — direct P2P for 2, SFU for 3+ — but do NOT build it in v1; ship the SFU path for everything, measure, then optimise. Building two media paths before you have users is how this feature becomes a swamp.

Second, Janus's AudioBridge plugin does server-side audio MIXING, so a participant receives one mixed stream rather than N. For a five-year-old and a sixty-eight-year-old on a variable Nigerian connection, an audio-first call that degrades gracefully is probably the feature that actually matters, more than video quality. No SFU here mixes audio by default — they all forward. If reliability on bad connections becomes the priority, "audio-only mode that mixes server-side" is a real architectural lever, and it is worth designing the UI so that dropping to audio feels like a normal warm choice rather than a failure state.

options.name: Cloudflare Realtime SFU + TURN
options.license: Service is proprietary/managed. The examples repo has NO LICENSE file at all (flagged — copy code from it at your own risk).
options.stars: 143 (examples repo only; there is no official SDK)
options.maintained: Service is GA (SFU and TURN both). Examples repo last pushed 2026-08-27; docs page updated 2026-08-27. Actively developed.
options.whatItDoes: Cloudflare's global anycast WebRTC plumbing: an SFU (media router for 3+ participants) and a managed TURN relay. You compose calls from WebRTC primitives yourself — publish/subscribe tracks over a REST API against your own RTCPeerConnection.
options.serverNeeded: No always-on service of ours. Needs a server-side secret holder: TURN credentials are minted by POSTing to https://rtc.live.cloudflare.com/v1/turn/keys/$KEY_ID/credentials/generate-ice-servers with a Bearer API token and a ttl. Cloudflare's docs explicitly say keep the TURN key server-side and hand the browser only short-lived credentials — that is exactly one Supabase edge function. Same pattern for SFU app secrets.
options.fitsUs: Best structural fit. Billing is per-GB, not per-minute, so cost does not scale with family count the way a SaaS seat/minute bill does. TURN is the piece we genuinely cannot avoid for Nigerian mobile carriers behind symmetric NAT, and it is FREE when used alongside the SFU (no double charge). Anycast means a Croydon↔Ibadan relay picks a near PoP rather than hairpinning through one region. CSP additions are modest and there is currently NO Content-Security-Policy block in businesses/wafe/vercel.json, so this is a new section, not a conflict.
options.cost: $0.05 per GB egress (Cloudflare→client only; inbound always free), with a 1,000 GB/month free tier SHARED across SFU and TURN — not two separate allowances. Rough arithmetic (mine, not Cloudflare's): a 2-person 720p call at ~1.5 Mbps each ≈ 22 MB per session-minute, so 1,000 GB ≈ 45,000 free session-minutes/month; audio-only is roughly 20-30x cheaper again. TURN only bills on calls that actually relay (typically a minority).
options.risks: The big one: NO official JavaScript SDK. You write track management, renegotiation, reconnection, device switching and the 30-second inactivity/garbage-collection handling yourself. That is real engineering, not glue. Other limits: 50 API calls/sec per session, tracks garbage-collected after 30s of no media, sessions recoverable for only 30s after connectivity loss (a Nigerian tunnel or lift will drop the call). The examples repo being unlicensed is a genuine legal snag if you lift code from it.

options.name: Cloudflare RealtimeKit (ex-Dyte)
options.repo: https://developers.cloudflare.com/realtime/realtimekit/ (no public source repo; Dyte team joined Cloudflare)
options.maintained: Announced and actively shipping, but CLOSED BETA — access by request. Free during beta.
options.whatItDoes: The batteries-included layer on top of Cloudflare Realtime: web SDKs (React, Angular, vanilla, WebComponents), mobile SDKs, prebuilt UI components, server-side recording/transcription. Everything the bare SFU makes you build.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours; meeting/participant tokens minted server-side from a Supabase edge function.
options.fitsUs: Would erase the SFU's build cost and give us React components immediately. Post-GA pricing is the cheapest per-minute of anything here by a wide margin, and the audio-only rate is the one that matters for a grandmother on a variable Nigerian connection.
options.cost: Free while in beta. At GA: $0.002/min audio+video participant, $0.0005/min audio-only participant, $0.010/min recording. Explicitly NO free tier at GA.
options.risks: Closed beta is the whole risk: no committed GA date, no SLA, terms can move, and we would not get access without asking. Building the Mama Fọláké call on a closed beta and then discovering there is no free tier at GA is precisely the 'free tier that expires' trap in the brief. Also the prebuilt UI is a corporate-meeting aesthetic by default — reskinning it to feel warm for a five-year-old is work you would not expect.

options.name: Daily.co
options.repo: https://github.com/daily-co (daily-js SDK; also authors Pipecat, which we already run)
options.license: Proprietary managed service (client SDKs are open, service is not)
options.maintained: Active. Same company that builds Pipecat, which already runs on our Oracle VM at voice.phoxta.com — so we have de facto familiarity with their stack.
options.whatItDoes: Full managed video/audio calling: prebuilt embeddable call UI plus a raw tracks API if you want to build your own. Best developer experience in this list.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours. Room creation and meeting tokens require the API key — a Supabase edge function, same pattern as everything else here. Never ship the key to the SPA.
options.fitsUs: Fastest credible path to a working call. The Pipecat overlap is a real, non-obvious advantage: if Wàfè ever wants an AI participant on a family call, that road is already paved. Raw-tracks mode means we can build our own warm UI rather than accepting theirs.
options.cost: 10,000 free participant-minutes/month, ongoing (not a trial), then $0.004 per participant-minute. Volume discounts down to $0.0015/min only at 50M+ min/month, which we will never see.
options.risks: The free tier is PER ACCOUNT, not per family — 10,000 participant-minutes is about 5,000 minutes of a 2-person call shared across every tenant on the marketplace. Roughly 80 families doing one hour-long call a month exhausts it, then every additional minute is metered. For a product sold to families this is the exact per-minute bill that attacks margin. Moderate lock-in: their room/token model is proprietary, though the client code is thin enough to replace.

options.name: 100ms
options.maintained: Active service; status page shows normal operations (a 10-min incident 2026-08-13). Company is small: ~70 staff, ~$5.6M estimated ARR.
options.whatItDoes: Managed video/audio conferencing with a well-regarded prebuilt React component kit and a headless SDK.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours; room codes and auth tokens minted server-side (Supabase edge function).
options.fitsUs: The audio-only discount is genuinely relevant to us: 75% off means about $0.001/min for the Mama Fọláké voice call, and audio-only is the right default on a variable connection. Prebuilt React UI is themeable.
options.cost: Free tier: 10,000 conferencing minutes/month plus 10,000 streaming minutes and 300 min each of recording/transcription. Then $0.004/participant-min video (SD/HD), $0.0012/min per streaming viewer, audio-only 75% off. Enterprise support is $2,500/month — ignore.
options.risks: Vendor durability is the honest concern: ~$5.6M ARR in a market where Cloudflare, Agora and LiveKit are all pushing hard. This is the option most likely to be acquired or repriced in the life of the product. Same per-account free-tier ceiling problem as Daily. Lock-in is moderate.

options.name: Agora
options.maintained: Active, publicly listed (NASDAQ: API), long-established. Lowest vendor-death risk of the pure-SaaS options.
options.whatItDoes: Mature global RTC network for voice/video, with its own SD-RTN transport designed for lossy and congested networks.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours. Channel tokens must be signed server-side with the App Certificate — a Supabase edge function.
options.fitsUs: The strongest case is network quality on exactly our route. Agora built its reputation on emerging-market connectivity and packet loss recovery, which is the Ibadan-on-mobile-data problem stated in the brief. If call quality to Nigeria turns out to be the thing that makes or breaks the feature, this is the one to bench against.
options.cost: 10,000 free minutes/month, ongoing (described as every month, not a trial). Then approximately: audio $0.99 per 1,000 participant-min ($0.00099/min), HD video $3.99/1,000 ($0.00399/min), Full HD $8.99/1,000. Volume discounts above 10k min.
options.risks: I could not load agora.io's own video-calling pricing page (404) — the per-1,000-minute figures above come from secondary sources and Agora's older docs, so treat them as approximate and re-verify before committing. Highest lock-in of the managed set: proprietary transport, proprietary signalling, no self-host path, and their SDK surface is large. Same per-account free-tier ceiling. Also a heavier client bundle than the alternatives.

options.name: Twilio Programmable Video
options.license: Proprietary managed service (JS SDK is open)
options.maintained: ALIVE — the brief's premise is out of date. Twilio announced EOL (moved to 5 Dec 2026) in March 2024, then publicly REVERSED it on 21 Oct 2024: 'we've reversed our earlier decision to retire Twilio Video in 2026… Twilio Video will remain a standalone product.' It is a supported GA product today.
options.whatItDoes: Managed group rooms (up to 50 participants) and P2P rooms, with recording.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours; access tokens signed server-side with an API key/secret — a Supabase edge function.
options.fitsUs: Poorly. It offers nothing the others don't, at the same or worse price, with no ongoing free tier.
options.cost: $0.004 per participant-minute for Group Rooms; recordings billed at the same rate again. Free TRIAL CREDIT only — there is no recurring monthly free allowance.
options.risks: Reputational/strategic: Twilio tried to kill this product once and only reversed under customer pressure. Building a consumer feature on a service the vendor has already publicly attempted to sunset is an avoidable risk when equivalents cost the same. No ongoing free tier means we pay from the very first Mama Fọláké call. Recommend ruling out.

options.name: LiveKit Cloud (and self-hosted LiveKit)
options.license: Apache-2.0 (server AND client SDKs) — the cleanest licence here
options.maintained: Very active — server pushed 2026-09-07, JS client 2026-09-03.
options.whatItDoes: Open-source WebRTC SFU with a managed cloud on top. Mature JS/React SDKs and prebuilt components. The only option where the identical software can run on their infrastructure or ours.
options.serverNeeded: Cloud: none of ours (JWT access tokens signed server-side — a Supabase edge function; the signing key must never reach the SPA). Self-hosted: a real always-on service — SFU plus a TURN/TLS setup plus Redis for multi-node — on the Oracle arm64 VM alongside Pipecat and worker-cron.
options.fitsUs: The best ANTI-LOCK-IN story by a distance: if cloud costs bite or the vendor repriced, the same Apache-2.0 server can move onto our own VM with no client rewrite. That optionality is worth real money on a product with a decade-long life. Against it: LiveKit's product focus has visibly pivoted to AI voice agents — their pricing page now leads entirely with agent minutes, STT and TTS. Plain human-to-human family conferencing is no longer the story they are telling.
options.cost: Build (free): 100 concurrent participants, 50 GB bandwidth, 5,000 connection-minutes/month, no card required. Then $0.12/GB DOWNSTREAM (upstream is free) plus a $0.0005/min connection fee per participant. Ship $50/mo = 250 GB + 150k minutes; Scale $500/mo = 3 TB + 1.5M minutes.
options.risks: The free tier is the smallest here in practice — 50 GB is roughly 2,200 minutes of a 2-person video call by my arithmetic, and the 5,000 connection-minutes cap binds even sooner. At $0.12/GB it is over twice Cloudflare's $0.05/GB. Self-hosting on the one small arm64 VM is possible but would put family calls on the same box as the voice server and cron worker — one noisy neighbour and everything degrades together. Be honest that self-hosting also means WE pay the TURN relay bandwidth.

options.name: Whereby Embedded
options.repo: No public source repo (proprietary; embed via iframe or their web component)
options.maintained: Active commercial product.
options.whatItDoes: Drop-in embedded video rooms — an iframe or web component and you have a working call, including chat, screenshare, waiting rooms and background effects, up to 200 participants.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours; room URLs created server-side via their REST API (Supabase edge function).
options.fitsUs: Fastest possible time-to-first-call — genuinely an afternoon. But the UI IS the product, and the brief asks for warm-not-corporate, role-aware and usable by a five-year-old. An iframe we cannot restructure is the direct opposite of that requirement. Also iframe embedding needs frame-src in the CSP, not just connect-src.
options.cost: Explore (free): 2,000 participant-minutes/month — the smallest allowance here. Build: $9.99/month including 2,000 minutes, then $0.004/participant-minute. Transcription $0.0065/min, recording $0.01/min.
options.risks: Highest lock-in of everything reviewed: we would own none of the call experience and could not make it feel like Wàfè. 2,000 free minutes is roughly 16 hour-long two-person calls across the ENTIRE marketplace per month. Reasonable as a throwaway prototype to prove the flow; wrong as a foundation.

options.name: Supabase Realtime + Postgres + Storage (build chat ourselves)
options.maintained: Very active — last pushed 2026-09-04. It is core Supabase infrastructure we already depend on.
options.whatItDoes: Everything family chat needs, from parts we already pay for. Postgres tables = message storage, history and offline catch-up (fetch where created_at > last_seen on reconnect). Realtime Broadcast = delivery, typing indicators and ephemeral signals that should never hit disk. Presence = who is online. Storage with RLS = attachments. Postgres Changes = live message inserts.
options.serverNeeded: NOTHING NEW. No additional container, no extra always-on process, no new vendor, no new failure mode. Moderation and any AI assistance ride on the existing edge functions and AI gateway.
options.fitsUs: This is the one that actually satisfies the product's stated spine, and it is not close. Supabase Realtime Authorization enforces RLS on PRIVATE broadcast and presence channels through policies on realtime.messages (with extension = 'broadcast' or 'presence'), so 'a child never sees something simply because they belong to the family' is expressed in the SAME policy language as the rest of Wàfè, evaluated in one place, on the user's existing Auth JWT. Every hosted-chat alternative would force us to mirror that privacy model into a second permission system and keep the two in sync forever — which is how children end up seeing things they shouldn't. Role-awareness (parent/child/guest), per-thread guest scoping for Mama Fọláké and Pastor Dayo, and child moderation are all just columns and policies. To make private channels actually private you must disable 'Allow public access' in Realtime Settings and open channels with { config: { private: true } } — easy to forget, so put it in the migration checklist.
options.cost: £0 additional on the existing Pro plan ($25/mo): 500 peak concurrent connections and 5 million Realtime messages/month included; overage $2.50 per million messages and $10 per 1,000 extra peak connections. Attachments come out of the 100 GB Storage already included. Free tier for reference: 200 connections, 100 msg/sec.
options.risks: We build it, so we own it — typing indicators, read receipts, reconnect/backfill, ordering and optimistic UI are each a day or two of careful work, and reconnect-on-a-flaky-Nigerian-connection is the part that will actually be hard. Hard limits to design against: 100 channels per connection (so use one channel per family, not one per conversation), broadcast payload 256 KB free / 3 MB Pro, 72-hour broadcast replay retention. No E2EE unless we build it. No moderation out of the box — for children that means we write it (a moderation column plus an edge function on the existing AI gateway). I did not verify exactly how broadcast messages versus postgres_changes count toward the 5M message quota — worth confirming before assuming headroom.

options.name: Matrix (element-hq/synapse + matrix-js-sdk)
options.license: Synapse AGPL-3.0 (relicensed from Apache in Nov 2023, dual-licensed commercially by Element); matrix-js-sdk is Apache-2.0
options.maintained: Genuinely active — synapse pushed 2026-09-04, matrix-js-sdk 2026-09-06. BUT NOTE: matrix-org/matrix-react-sdk is ARCHIVED (last push 2024-09-11, merged into element-web). Most Matrix-in-React tutorials online point at that archived repo — a real trap.
options.whatItDoes: A federated, end-to-end-encrypted messaging protocol with a reference homeserver. Real E2EE, real decentralisation, VoIP signalling built into the spec.
options.serverNeeded: A LOT. Synapse is a Python/Twisted + Rust homeserver requiring its own Postgres, a media store, TLS, .well-known delegation, and ongoing security patching — plus coturn for its calling. Putting that on the one small arm64 Oracle VM next to Pipecat and worker-cron is not something I would call honest operations.
options.fitsUs: Badly, despite being technically impressive. Two disqualifiers. First, identity: Matrix users are not Supabase Auth users, so the privacy model would live in TWO systems — Synapse's power levels and room membership AND our RLS — and would drift. That directly undermines the product's central privacy promise. Second, E2EE and child moderation are in tension: if we cannot read messages we cannot screen them for a five-year-old, and Matrix's device-verification UX defeats a sixty-eight-year-old on a phone in Ibadan. Federation is a feature Wàfè does not want — families should not be discoverable across servers.
options.cost: Software free. Real cost is operational: a dedicated VM (Synapse is memory-hungry and grows state indefinitely), Postgres, backups, media storage, TLS renewal, and a standing security-patch obligation. Realistically the largest total cost on this list.
options.risks: AGPL-3.0 is fine for self-hosting (no distribution, so no copyleft trigger) but Element's dual-licence strategy signals more monetisation pressure ahead. Synapse state growth and room-join performance are long-standing operational complaints. Federation is an attack surface we would have to actively disable. And the archived matrix-react-sdk means the React integration path is less well-trodden than it looks. Recommend ruling out.

options.name: Rocket.Chat
options.license: MIT for the core, BUT the ee/ and apps/meteor/ee/ directories are under a separate proprietary licence (this is why GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Verified by reading the LICENSE file directly.
options.maintained: Very active — pushed 2026-09-06.
options.whatItDoes: A complete self-hosted Slack/Teams alternative: channels, threads, omnichannel, apps, video conferencing integrations.
options.serverNeeded: Node.js/Meteor plus MongoDB, always on, plus a reverse proxy — a second stateful database alongside our Postgres, on the small arm64 VM.
options.fitsUs: Wrong shape entirely. This is an APPLICATION, not a chat library — you deploy Rocket.Chat and embed or iframe it, you do not compose it into a React app. The UI is workplace team-chat: channels, mentions, admin panels. Asking a five-year-old to use it, or asking Mama Fọláké to learn it, misses the brief completely. And again it brings its own users and permissions, duplicating the privacy model outside RLS.
options.cost: Self-hosted community edition free, but MongoDB hosting plus the VM headroom is real money and real operational load. Cloud plans start in the tens of dollars per workspace per month, which does not fit a per-family marketplace product at all.
options.risks: Second database technology to operate and back up. The MIT/ee split means features can and do migrate behind the enterprise licence. Heavy resource footprint. Not embeddable in the way we would need. Recommend ruling out.

options.name: Chatwoot
options.license: MIT core with a proprietary enterprise/ directory (again why GitHub says NOASSERTION). Verified by reading the LICENSE file.
options.maintained: Very active — pushed 2026-09-06.
options.whatItDoes: Open-source customer-support / shared-inbox software: support AGENTS answer inbound CUSTOMERS across web widget, email, WhatsApp and social channels.
options.serverNeeded: Ruby on Rails plus Postgres plus Redis plus Sidekiq — an always-on multi-process stack.
options.fitsUs: It does not. Chatwoot's data model is agent↔customer conversations in an inbox, which is asymmetric support ticketing. Wàfè needs symmetric peer chat among family members with role-aware visibility. Modelling Dami (15) as a 'customer' and Ifeoluwa as a 'support agent' would be fighting the software forever. Worth stating plainly since it was named in the brief: it is the right tool for the Phoxta operating console (where it overlaps with the Inbox module we already built), and the wrong tool for a family.
options.cost: Self-hosted free; cloud from roughly $19-39 per AGENT per month — a seat model, which is exactly the pricing shape that breaks on a consumer family product.
options.risks: Fundamental model mismatch, plus a heavy Rails/Redis/Sidekiq footprint we would be operating for no benefit. Recommend ruling out.

options.name: Stream Chat (getstream.io)
options.license: Proprietary service; the React SDK repo reports NOASSERTION (Stream's own licence, not OSI)
options.maintained: Active — pushed 2026-09-03. Well-resourced, low vendor-death risk.
options.whatItDoes: Best-in-class hosted chat API: message storage, delivery, typing indicators, read receipts, reactions, threads, attachments, push, and BUILT-IN AI moderation — every checkbox in the brief, working on day one.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours; user tokens signed server-side with the API secret (Supabase edge function).
options.fitsUs: Technically the fastest and most feature-complete answer, and its moderation tooling is a genuine advantage for a product with children in it — that is the one thing it does better than anything we would build. But the pricing model is fatal for us, and it would relocate the privacy model into Stream's channel/role permission system, permanently duplicating the thing RLS already does correctly.
options.cost: Build (free): 1,000 MAU and 100 concurrent connections. Maker account: $100/month credit, but only for teams under 5 people with under $10k monthly revenue and 'availability is limited'. Then the cliff: Start is $399/month (billed annually) for 10,000 MAU, Elevate $599/month; overages $0.07-$0.09 per MAU.
options.risks: THE FREE TIER IS A TRAP FOR THIS PRODUCT. Every family member is a monthly active user, so a five-person family plus two guests is roughly 7 MAU — about 140 families and we fall off the free tier straight onto a $399/month floor. That is a step function, not a curve, and it lands long before the revenue to pay for it. The Maker plan explicitly disappears the moment Wàfè succeeds. Plus proprietary licence, message data living in Stream's cloud (awkward for a privacy-first family product), and a second permission model to keep in sync. Recommend ruling out.

recommendation:
Build chat on Supabase; rent only the calling media path, from Cloudflare — and stage it so the Mama Fọláké call ships without a new vendor at all.

CHAT — build on Supabase Realtime + Postgres + Storage. This is not the cheap answer, it is the correct one. The brief's hardest requirement is "a child never sees something simply because they belong to the family," and Supabase Realtime Authorization enforces RLS on private broadcast and presence channels via policies on realtime.messages, evaluated against the same Auth JWT as everything else in Wàfè. Every alternative — Stream, Matrix, Rocket.Chat — forces us to mirror that privacy model into a second permission system and keep the two in sync forever, which is precisely how a fifteen-year-old ends up reading a thread about her own guardianship. One policy language, one place, one audit. Postgres gives storage, history and offline backfill; broadcast gives typing indicators without writing them to disk; presence gives who's-online; Storage (100 GB already on Pro) gives attachments under the same RLS. Cost: £0 additional. Moderation for children is the one thing we must write ourselves, and it should ride the existing AI gateway with assertWithinCap + meter, as every AI feature here does.

CALLING — stage it, because the demo calendar event only needs two people.

Phase 1, the Mama Fọláké call (1:1, and up to ~3): plain browser WebRTC peer-to-peer, using Supabase Realtime broadcast as the signalling channel — already RLS-authorised, already paid for, no new vendor, no new failure mode — plus Cloudflare Realtime TURN for the NAT traversal that WILL be required on Nigerian mobile carriers. That answers the brief's "who pays for TURN" question honestly: Cloudflare does, up to 1,000 GB/month, and only for the minority of calls that actually relay. On the P2P path, media never touches a third party at all, which is the right story for a privacy-first family product.

Phase 2, the whole family calling Ibadan (4+): P2P mesh collapses at four participants, so add Cloudflare Realtime SFU — same account, same credentials, same 1,000 GB bucket, same edge function. At $0.05/GB against LiveKit's $0.12/GB and everyone else's $0.004/participant-minute, bandwidth billing is the only model that does not scale punitively with the number of families on the marketplace. Cloudflare SFU and TURN are both GA, not beta.

The honest cost of that choice is that Cloudflare ships no JavaScript SDK — we write track management, renegotiation, reconnection and device handling ourselves, against 30-second track garbage-collection and a 30-second session recovery window. Budget for that properly; it is the single biggest unknown in this plan.

Two escape hatches, both real: if the no-SDK burden proves worse than estimated, Daily.co (10,000 free participant-min/month, then $0.004/min) gets working calls in a day and we already run their Pipecat framework on the Oracle VM. If we later want to own the whole stack, LiveKit is Apache-2.0 on both server and client and can move onto our own hardware without a client rewrite. Bench Agora only if call quality to Nigeria turns out to be the binding constraint — that is the one thing they are genuinely better at.

Rule out: Whereby (an iframe cannot be made warm, and 2,000 min/month is 16 calls across the whole marketplace), Twilio Video (no ongoing free tier, and a vendor that already tried to kill it once), Stream Chat (a $399/month cliff at roughly 140 families), Matrix/Synapse (duplicate identity model, E2EE fights child moderation, and it needs a VM we cannot honestly spare), Rocket.Chat and Chatwoot (both are applications with the wrong shape — workplace chat and support ticketing respectively). RealtimeKit is the one to watch: at $0.002/min A/V and $0.0005/min audio-only it would be the cheapest managed option and comes with React components, but it is closed beta with no GA date and explicitly no free tier at GA. Do not build on it yet; do request access and re-evaluate before Phase 2.
notes:
CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: Twilio Programmable Video is NOT being sunset. Twilio announced EOL (moved to 5 Dec 2026) in March 2024, then publicly reversed it on 21 Oct 2024 — "Twilio Video will remain a standalone product." Verified on Twilio's own changelog. It is still not worth choosing, but for pricing reasons, not mortality.

VERIFIED FROM PRIMARY SOURCES: Cloudflare SFU/TURN pricing and the 1,000 GB shared free tier (developers.cloudflare.com/realtime/sfu/pricing); Cloudflare SFU limits — 50 API calls/sec/session, 30s track GC, 30s session recovery (realtime/sfu/limits); Cloudflare TURN credential minting endpoint and the keep-the-key-server-side rule (realtime/turn/generate-credentials); SFU+TURN GA vs RealtimeKit closed beta (Cloudflare's own launch blog); Supabase Realtime quotas and Realtime Authorization via RLS on realtime.messages (supabase.com/docs); Supabase Pro pricing (supabase.com/pricing); Whereby, 100ms, Daily and Twilio pricing pages; LiveKit's own pricing blog post. Repo metadata (stars, licence, archived flag, last push) pulled live from the GitHub API on 2026-09-07 — all thirteen candidates verified non-archived and pushed within the last four days, EXCEPT matrix-org/matrix-react-sdk, which IS archived (last push 2024-09-11). Rocket.Chat and Chatwoot licences read directly from their LICENSE files, confirming MIT core plus proprietary ee//enterprise/ directories.

NOT VERIFIED — treat with caution:
- Agora's per-1,000-minute rates. Their video-calling pricing URL returned 404 and the figures ($0.99 audio / $3.99 HD / $8.99 Full HD per 1,000 min) come from secondary sources. Re-check before committing.
- Whether Daily's free tier requires a card on file. Their pricing page does not say.
- Exactly how Supabase counts a "message" against the 5M/month Pro allowance — specifically whether broadcast messages and postgres_changes events are metered the same way, and whether a message fanned out to five family members counts once or five times. This materially changes the headroom estimate and should be confirmed with Supabase before we design around it.
- RealtimeKit closed-beta access. I did not request or confirm we could get it, and no GA date is published.
- Whether Cloudflare's TURN free allowance is genuinely shared with SFU in both directions of the bundle. The docs say the 1,000 GB covers both and that SFU↔TURN traffic is not double-charged, but the exact accounting when TURN is used STANDALONE (our Phase 1) is worth confirming with Cloudflare — that is the case we would actually be running first.

MY OWN ARITHMETIC, NOT VENDOR FIGURES: all GB↔minutes conversions in this report are mine, assuming roughly 1.5 Mbps per 720p video stream and counting downstream only. That gives ~22 MB per session-minute for a 2-person call, hence ~45,000 free session-minutes on Cloudflare's 1,000 GB and ~2,200 on LiveKit's 50 GB. Real bitrates vary with resolution, simulcast layers and network adaptation — treat these as order-of-magnitude, and measure before relying on them.

REPO OBSERVATION: businesses/wafe/vercel.json currently contains NO Content-Security-Policy block at all. Adding third-party origins is therefore a new section rather than an edit to an existing policy — but note that means Wàfè is also shipping without a CSP today, which is worth raising separately from this decision. Wàfè already depends on @supabase/supabase-js ^2.108.2, React 19 and Vite 6, so the chat recommendation adds no new dependency whatsoever.

ONE THING NOBODY ASKED BUT SOMEONE SHOULD: the brief names WhatsApp as a tool Wàfè replaces. Mama Fọláké, 68, in Ibadan, almost certainly already has WhatsApp working and does not want a new app. Whatever we build, the join-a-call path for a guest must survive her not installing anything and not creating an account — a signed, expiring link that opens straight into a call in mobile Safari or Chrome. That constraint should drive the calling choice as hard as price does, and it is an argument for the P2P/Cloudflare path (a plain web page we control) over any SDK whose join flow assumes an app install or an account.

options.name: Raw RTCPeerConnection (no library) + "perfect negotiation"
options.license: n/a — browser API, no dependency, no licence
options.maintained: It is the platform. caniuse: RTCPeerConnection supported Safari 11+, iOS Safari 11+, Chrome 23+, Firefox 22+; current as of Safari 26.6 / Chrome 154 / Firefox 157 (verified against caniuse features-json).
options.whatItDoes: You create RTCPeerConnection yourself, call getUserMedia, add tracks, and shuttle SDP offers/answers and ICE candidates over whatever transport you like. The "perfect negotiation" pattern (polite/impolite peer + ignoreOffer + makingOffer flags) removes the glare race that every naive implementation hits, and setLocalDescription() with no arguments auto-generates the right answer. ~150-250 lines for a useCall() hook covering 1:1 plus a peer map for mesh.
options.serverNeeded: Signalling only. No media server. Signalling = Supabase Realtime broadcast on a PRIVATE channel (verified working — see notes). TURN credentials minted by a Supabase edge function. Zero new always-on infrastructure.
options.fitsUs: Best fit. Nothing to bundle, nothing to polyfill, no Node shims in Vite, TypeScript types come from lib.dom.d.ts so `strict` is satisfied natively. Signalling rides Supabase Realtime, which we already pay for and which already carries our presence. Crucially, privacy is enforced where our other privacy is enforced: an RLS policy on realtime.messages decides who may even see a call offer, so a child cannot receive a ring for a conversation they are not part of — that is not achievable with any library that owns its own signalling channel.
options.cost: £0 in libraries and £0 in signalling beyond existing Supabase usage. Only TURN relay costs money.
options.risks: Most code to write and own: renegotiation on track replace, ICE restart on network change (a Nigerian phone switching cell to Wi-Fi WILL drop the connection without iceRestart handling), connectionstatechange recovery, and the mesh bookkeeping. These are exactly the bugs the libraries exist to have already fixed, so budget real time for them, and read Trystero's peer.mjs as the worked answer rather than inventing it.

options.name: Trystero + @trystero-p2p/supabase
options.stars: Not verified — the GitHub API rate-limited me mid-research; I did not want to quote a number I had not read. npm publish cadence below is the maintenance evidence I actually confirmed.
options.maintained: Actively maintained. npm 0.25.4 published 2026-08-30; the five most recent main-branch commits are all 2026-08-30 (nostr relay pruning/timeouts). Single principal maintainer (dmotz).
options.whatItDoes: Room-based P2P: joinRoom(config, roomId) gives you onPeerJoin/onPeerLeave, addStream/addTrack/replaceTrack for audio+video, and makeAction() for typed data channels — i.e. it covers BOTH halves of "Together" (calls and chat/data) in one API. Signalling is pluggable across seven strategies (BitTorrent, Nostr, MQTT, Supabase, Firebase, IPFS, self-hosted WS relay). SDP is encrypted in transit by a key derived from appId+roomId, with an optional shared `password`. Ships real TypeScript declarations; ESM with per-strategy entry points so you only bundle the one you import.
options.serverNeeded: None beyond Supabase. I read the published source of @trystero-p2p/supabase@0.25.4: it does `client.channel('room:<topic>:messages')` and `chan.send({type:'broadcast', event:'sdp'|'join', payload})`. That is a shipping, third-party proof that Supabase Realtime broadcast carries the full offer/answer/ICE exchange.
options.fitsUs: Very good as a prototype accelerator and as a reference implementation. Bundle is small: the Supabase strategy dist is 3.5 KB and the core is ~40 KB of raw (unminified, ungzipped) ESM split across peer/room/media/handshake modules, tree-shaken per strategy. It would get a working Ifeoluwa-to-Mama-Fọláké call up in a day.
options.cost: £0, MIT.
options.risks: Two concrete problems for OUR privacy model, both read from the source, not inferred. (1) It creates its OWN Supabase client — `let client = null; init: config => client ||= createClient(config.appId, config.relayConfig.supabaseKey)` — so it opens a SECOND Realtime websocket alongside our app's client, doubling our count against the 200 concurrent-connection free-plan cap and holding no session of ours. (2) It uses PUBLIC broadcast channels (`broadcast: {self:false}`, no `private: true`), so authorisation is not RLS — it is "knows the anon key + the room id", with SDP confidentiality resting on Trystero's own appId+roomId-derived encryption. That is a fundamentally different trust model from "a child never sees something simply because they belong to the family". Also bus-factor one.

options.name: simple-peer (feross)
options.maintained: NO. Effectively abandoned. Last commit 2022-02-17; last npm publish 9.11.1 on 2022-02-17 — four and a half years. 128 open issues. Registry metadata last touched 2023-01-26. Not archived and NOT flagged deprecated on npm, so it looks alive on a casual glance — that is the trap.
options.whatItDoes: A small stream-flavoured wrapper over RTCPeerConnection: `new Peer({initiator})`, emits 'signal' (you ferry that blob to the other side), 'stream', 'data'. Genuinely nice ergonomics for 1:1.
options.serverNeeded: Signalling only, bring your own — Supabase broadcast would work fine.
options.fitsUs: Poorly, for a mechanical reason beyond the staleness. Its dependencies are Node-isms — buffer, readable-stream, randombytes, get-browser-rtc, queue-microtask, err-code, debug (verified from the 9.11.1 manifest). Under Vite 6 that means adding node polyfills (vite-plugin-node-polyfills or manual aliases) to ship a browser bundle, and shipping `buffer` + `readable-stream` for a video call. simplepeer.min.js is 99,448 bytes minified before gzip. It also ships no TypeScript types, so `strict` needs the community @types/simple-peer.
options.risks: Any bug you hit in 2026 — and iOS Safari changes annually — is yours to fork around, because nobody is merging your PR. Recommend against.

options.name: @thaunknown/simple-peer (the maintained fork)
options.maintained: Yes, quietly. npm 10.1.2 published 2026-07-25; commits 2026-07-25, 2026-05-21, 2026-01-15 — mostly dependency bumps rather than feature work.
options.whatItDoes: API-compatible with feross/simple-peer but modernised: drops node:stream and node:buffer for streamx and Uint8Array (deps: debug, err-code, streamx, uint8-util, webrtc-polyfill). 98 KB unpacked.
options.serverNeeded: Signalling only, bring your own.
options.fitsUs: It fixes the Vite polyfill problem, which is the main reason to prefer it over the original. But it is a 39-star fork maintained by one person as a by-product of their torrent client, and — verified from the manifest — it still declares no `types` entry, so TypeScript strict needs hand-written declarations.
options.risks: Bus factor of one at a 39-star project is a worse bet than owning ~200 lines ourselves. If we were going to depend on someone's wrapper we should depend on Trystero, which is better maintained and does more.

options.name: PeerJS (peers/peerjs) + peerjs-server
options.maintained: Semi. peerjs 1.5.5 published 2025-06-07 — ~15 months old. Recent repo commits are Renovate dependency chores (latest content commits Jul 2025). 201 open issues. The v2 rewrite is a corpse: 2.0.0-beta.3 was published 2022-02-21 and there has been no beta.4 in four and a half years. peerjs-server is in similar shape — repo dep-chores to Aug 2025, but the npm package `peer` is stuck at 1.0.2 from 2023-12-05.
options.whatItDoes: Highest-level API of the lot: every peer gets an id, `peer.call(id, stream)` and `peer.connect(id)` do the rest. Deps: @msgpack/msgpack, eventemitter3, peerjs-js-binarypack, webrtc-adapter. peerjs.min.js is 86,948 bytes minified pre-gzip. Ships its own .d.ts.
options.serverNeeded: THIS IS THE DISQUALIFIER. PeerJS is architecturally coupled to a PeerServer — a long-lived Node/Express/ws process for id brokering and signalling. We have no Node server in front of the SPA, so it goes on the Oracle VM: a third always-on service beside Pipecat and worker-cron, with its own websocket scaling, TLS, restart policy and CSP origin. The free hosted 0.peerjs.com cloud exists and is exactly the trap the brief warns about — unmetered, best-effort, no SLA, shared id space, and if it goes down the grandmother's call goes down with it.
options.fitsUs: Badly. It duplicates a transport we already run (Supabase Realtime) as a service we would have to operate, and it puts authorisation in a Node process instead of in RLS beside the rest of Wàfè's privacy model.
options.cost: £0 in licence; the real cost is a permanent operational surface on the Oracle box.
options.risks: Stalled v2, dependency-chore-only maintenance on v1, and a mandatory server. Recommend against.

options.name: Cloudflare Realtime TURN
options.maintained: Yes — actively developed Cloudflare product.
options.whatItDoes: Managed global TURN relay. Listens on STUN/UDP 3478 and 53, TURN/UDP 3478 and 53, TURN/TCP 3478 and 80, TURN/TLS 5349 and 443. The TLS-on-443 endpoint is the one that matters for us: it is what gets a call out of a Nigerian mobile carrier CGNAT or a locked-down office network that drops UDP.
options.serverNeeded: One Supabase edge function. Credentials are short-lived and minted server-side: POST https://rtc.live.cloudflare.com/v1/turn/keys/$TURN_KEY_ID/credentials/generate-ice-servers with a Bearer API token and a `ttl`, returning a ready-made iceServers array. The token must never reach the browser, so this is a ~30-line edge function — the same shape as our existing secret-holding functions.
options.fitsUs: Best TURN option by a distance. Docs state a free tier of 1,000 GB before charges, then $0.05 per GB of egress to the TURN client, and TURN is usable standalone without their SFU ("if your use case is one-to-one communication... TURN by itself is usually sufficient"). Per-allocation ceilings are >50-100 Mbps and >5-10 kpps — vastly above a family video call. Runs on Cloudflare's global network, excluding China; Nigeria and the UK are both well served.
options.cost: 1,000 GB/month free, then $0.05/GB. Sanity check: a 1:1 video call at ~1 Mbps each way relays roughly 450 MB per hour, so the free tier is on the order of 2,000+ relayed call-hours per month across ALL tenants, and beyond it a relayed call-hour costs about £0.02. Direct P2P calls cost nothing at all. Credentials can be refreshed mid-call via RTCPeerConnection.setConfiguration().
options.risks: It IS usage-scaling spend, which the brief rightly distrusts — but it scales only with RELAYED minutes, not all minutes, and only above 1,000 GB. Add a per-family monthly relayed-GB cap in our own metering (we already have assertWithinCap) so a runaway cannot bill us. UNVERIFIED: I could not confirm from the docs whether enabling Realtime TURN requires a card on file or a Workers Paid plan — check in the dashboard before committing.

options.name: Open Relay Project / metered.ca
options.maintained: Service is live and marketed as of 2026.
options.whatItDoes: Free shared TURN/STUN at openrelay.metered.ca on ports 80 and 443, TCP and UDP, with geo-routing. Signup for an API key, then fetch credentials from https://<app>.metered.live/api/v1/turn/credentials.
options.serverNeeded: None; an edge function to hold the API key.
options.fitsUs: Only as a secondary ICE entry behind Cloudflare.
options.cost: CONTRADICTORY, and this is the flag. The Open Relay marketing page says 20 GB of free TURN usage every month. Metered's own product pricing page at metered.ca/stun-turn says the free tier is 500 MB per month, with the first paid tier at $99/month for 150 GB ($0.40/GB overage), $199 for 500 GB, $499 for 2 TB. Those cannot both describe the same account.
options.risks: Exactly the "free tier that will bite us" pattern. Either the shared Open Relay pool is a separate best-effort service from the metered product (likely) or the free allowance has been cut by 40x. On the shared pool you are also sharing a public relay with everyone else's traffic, with no SLA. Do not put a grandmother's weekly call on it as the primary path; verify the real allowance in a dashboard before relying on it at all. Note also that the $99 first paid step is a cliff, not a ramp — one busy month and it is $99, versus Cloudflare's smooth $0.05/GB.

options.name: ExpressTURN
options.maintained: Live and listed alongside Cloudflare/Twilio/Metered/Xirsys in 2026 provider comparisons.
options.whatItDoes: Free TURN with a stated 1,000 GB/month allowance, TCP and UDP on port 3478, across a dozen-plus regions including Africa and Europe.
options.serverNeeded: None.
options.fitsUs: Marginal. The free tier is generous on paper, but per the sources the free plan is port 3478 only — no TLS/443 — which removes precisely the capability we need it for on a restrictive Nigerian mobile network.
options.cost: Free at 1,000 GB/month.
options.risks: Opaque operator with thin reputational signal (a 73/100 Scamadviser score is not a reference), no SLA, and we would be routing family video through it. At most a third-choice ICE fallback, never the primary.

options.name: Self-hosted coturn on the Oracle VM
options.license: BSD-3-Clause (Citrix; GitHub reports NOASSERTION because of the combined LICENSE file — I read the header to confirm)
options.maintained: Yes, vigorously — commits on 2026-09-06 (hiredis async cleanup, SASLprep control-character fix, ChannelBind allocation-mismatch fix). 305 open issues on a project this size is normal. This is the reference TURN implementation.
options.whatItDoes: Full STUN/TURN server, RFC 5766/8656, with long-term and REST/time-limited (HMAC) credentials, TLS, and configurable relay port ranges. Packaged for Ubuntu arm64, so it installs on our existing box.
options.serverNeeded: Our Oracle Cloud arm64 VM, alongside Pipecat and worker-cron.
options.fitsUs: It is genuinely possible and the bandwidth economics are the best available: Oracle Always Free includes 10 TB/month of outbound transfer, which dwarfs the relay traffic a family app would generate. If TURN spend ever became the binding cost, this is the escape hatch.
options.cost: £0 marginal, within the existing VM and its 10 TB egress.
options.risks: Be honest about what we would be taking on. A third always-on service on a small shared box, competing for CPU with a Pipecat voice server that has hard real-time requirements — relayed media is a steady packet flow, and a saturated VM degrades BOTH. Firewalling is the classic silent failure: 3478/5349 plus a large UDP relay range (typically 49152-65535) must be opened in the OCI security list AND in the instance's own iptables/nftables, and missing either produces calls that fail only for the users who need TURN — the exact users you cannot reproduce locally. Plus TLS cert renewal, coturn config drift, and single-region topology: a relay in one place adds a hop, though for Wàfè that is moot since one party is always in Croydon. My recommendation: install it later as a cost-control fallback, not now as the primary.

options.name: Supabase Realtime broadcast as the signalling channel
options.maintained: Yes — actively developed; binary payload support landed in supabase-js 2.91.0+.
options.whatItDoes: VERIFIED as viable for WebRTC signalling, both from the docs and from reading a shipping implementation. API shape: `supabase.channel('call:<id>', {config:{broadcast:{self:false}, private:true}})`, then `.on('broadcast', {event:'sdp'}, cb).subscribe()` and `.send({type:'broadcast', event:'sdp', payload})`. Arbitrary JSON payloads; `ack:true` confirms server receipt; messages sent before subscribe go over HTTP, after subscribe over the websocket. Presence on the same channel gives us who-is-available for free.
options.serverNeeded: None. This is the whole point — it is the piece that lets us have calls with no server of our own.
options.fitsUs: It is the keystone of the recommendation, and it is the piece that makes the privacy requirement achievable. Use `private: true` channels with an RLS policy on realtime.messages plus `await supabase.realtime.setAuth()`, so eligibility to receive a ring is decided by the same policy layer as everything else in Wàfè. Role-awareness (parent/child/guest) becomes a SQL predicate, not client-side branching a curious 15-year-old can inspect in devtools.
options.cost: Within existing Supabase spend. Free plan limits: 200 concurrent connections, 100 messages/sec, 100 channel joins/sec, 100 channels per connection, 256 KB broadcast payload (3,000 KB on paid). Billing: 2M messages/month included, then $2.50 per million. A whole call setup — offer, answer, and trickled ICE candidates — is on the order of 20-60 small messages per peer pair, so signalling volume is negligible; chat message volume will dominate long before call setup does.
options.risks: Two to watch. (1) Message accounting is per-recipient: one broadcast to a 5-person room counts as 6 messages (1 sent + 5 received), so a busy family chat multiplies faster than it looks. (2) The docs do not state clearly whether "messages per second" is scoped per client or per project — the error guidance says "your project is generating too many messages per second", which reads project-wide. At 100/sec on the free plan that is fine for a family app but worth confirming with Supabase before we sell to many families on one project. Also note the 200-connection cap is the real ceiling on concurrent tenants, and anything that opens a second Realtime socket per user halves it.

recommendation:
Write directly against RTCPeerConnection using the perfect-negotiation pattern, signal over Supabase Realtime PRIVATE broadcast channels guarded by RLS on realtime.messages, and use Cloudflare Realtime TURN with short-lived credentials minted by a Supabase edge function. Use Trystero as the reference implementation to read and prototype against, not as a production dependency.

The reasoning is short. Every library in this lane exists to solve one problem — you have a signalling transport, here is a nicer wrapper over RTCPeerConnection — and each charges a different price for it. simple-peer charges four and a half years of abandonment plus Node polyfills in Vite. PeerJS charges a Node server we would have to run on the Oracle box, duplicating a transport we already operate, and moving authorisation out of RLS. Trystero charges a second Supabase websocket and public, non-RLS channels. Meanwhile the thing all three wrap is about 200 lines of well-documented browser API.

The privacy requirement is what actually decides it. "A child never sees something simply because they belong to the family" is only enforceable if eligibility to receive a call offer is a database policy rather than a client-side check. Supabase private channels with RLS on realtime.messages give us exactly that — parent, child and guest become predicates in SQL, evaluated server-side, in the same place as the rest of Wàfè's privacy model. No library that owns its own signalling channel can give us that, and retrofitting it is harder than not needing to.

The cost shape is also right. Chat is Postgres plus Realtime, which we already pay for. Calls are free whenever peers connect directly, and only relayed calls consume TURN — Cloudflare's 1,000 GB free tier is on the order of 2,000+ relayed call-hours a month across all tenants, and beyond that a relayed call-hour is roughly two pence. Cap relayed GB per family through the existing assertWithinCap metering and there is no runaway. If TURN spend ever became the binding constraint, coturn on the Oracle VM with its 10 TB free egress is a real escape hatch — but install it as a cost-control fallback later, not as a third always-on service today competing with Pipecat for CPU on a small arm64 box.

Concretely, for the Adeyemis: a Croydon-to-Ibadan 1:1 video call is the primary case and mesh topology is irrelevant to it. Cap video mesh at 4 participants and degrade to audio-only beyond that — the binding constraint is that in a 5-way mesh every phone uploads 4 simultaneous video streams, which a Nigerian mobile uplink will not do. Build 1:1 first, make "Video call with Mama Fọláké at 14:00" a real button on that calendar event, and treat group video as a later, explicitly capped feature.
notes:
WHAT I VERIFIED DIRECTLY (not from summaries): npm registry `time` objects for simple-peer, peerjs, trystero and the forks; GitHub API repo metadata and commit dates for simple-peer, peerjs, peerjs-server, coturn; the coturn LICENSE header; caniuse features-json for RTCPeerConnection; jsdelivr file sizes for the peerjs and trystero dist bundles; and the published source of @trystero-p2p/supabase@0.25.4, which is where the "Supabase Realtime broadcast can carry SDP" claim comes from — it literally calls chan.send({type:'broadcast', event:'sdp', payload}) on a channel named room:<topic>:messages. That is a working proof, not a hopeful reading of the docs.

THINGS I COULD NOT CONFIRM AND YOU SHOULD CHECK BEFORE COMMITTING:
1. Whether Cloudflare Realtime TURN can be enabled on a free Cloudflare account, or needs a card / Workers Paid plan.
