The docs state the 1,000 GB free tier and the $0.05/GB rate but are silent on plan prerequisites. Ten minutes in the dashboard settles it, and it is load-bearing for the recommendation.
2. The Open Relay free allowance. metered.ca/tools/openrelay says 20 GB/month; metered.ca/stun-turn says 500 MB/month with the first paid step at $99. I could not reconcile these and I am not going to guess which is current. Treat Open Relay as unverified until someone reads it off a real dashboard.
3. Whether Supabase's "messages per second" limit is per client or per project. The limits table does not say; the error guidance implies project-wide. At our volumes it does not bite yet, but it changes the multi-tenant ceiling and is worth asking support.
4. Trystero's star count — the GitHub API rate-limited me and I would rather report nothing than a remembered number.

iOS SAFARI, SPECIFICALLY, because two of our users are on phones and one is five years old:
- RTCPeerConnection has been supported since iOS 11 and is current through iOS Safari 26.6. The baseline is not the problem; the platform quirks are.
- WebKit does not support capturing multiple video sources. A second getUserMedia video request STOPS the first, and a previously granted track's `muted` goes true with no programmatic way to unmute. Design for exactly one getUserMedia call, held in a ref, reused everywhere.
- Remote audio and video need playsInline and a user gesture before they will play. Any "auto-answer" or "join silently" flow will produce a black square and silence on iPhone. Make answering an explicit tap — which is also the right design for a five-year-old.
- There is a long-standing WebKit bug (bugs.webkit.org #252465) where a video element inside a home-screen PWA cannot play a getUserMedia stream. Ship Together as a normal browser tab, or test the standalone PWA path exhaustively before promising it. Separately, Apple removed standalone PWA mode in the EU under the DMA in 2024 — the UK is not affected, so Croydon is fine, but note it if Wàfè ever sells into the EU.

CSP: WebRTC's own media path (ICE/STUN/TURN/DTLS/SRTP) is not governed by connect-src, so the relay traffic itself needs no vercel.json change. What DOES need declaring is any fetch the page makes — and if you mint TURN credentials in an edge function as recommended, that is just our existing Supabase origin, so possibly no CSP change at all. Do NOT call rtc.live.cloudflare.com from the browser; that would both leak the API token and add a CSP origin. Low-confidence aside I did not verify: CSP Level 3 defines a `webrtc 'allow'|'block'` directive implemented in Chromium — if any of our vercel.json policies set it to block, WebRTC dies silently. Worth a grep before debugging anything else.

ONE THING NOBODY WILL BUDGET FOR: ICE restart. A phone in Ibadan moving between cell and Wi-Fi, or a carrier rotating its NAT binding, will kill an established connection. Handle `connectionstatechange` going to 'disconnected'/'failed' by calling setLocalDescription({iceRestart:true}) and re-signalling. This is the single most common reason hand-rolled WebRTC "works in testing, fails with Grandma", and it is the strongest argument for reading Trystero's peer.mjs before writing our own — the library authors have already paid for this lesson.

FINALLY, A HONEST CAVEAT ON RELAY RATES: the commonly cited figure is that 10-20% of calls require TURN. I did not verify that against a primary source and our UK-to-Nigeria mobile profile is probably worse than the average. Instrument it — log the selected candidate pair type per call — rather than assuming, because that ratio is the entire difference between "TURN is free forever" and "TURN is a line item".

options.name: jitsi/jitsi-meet — reference implementation for guest join-by-link
options.maintained: Yes — very active; last push 6 Sep 2026 (checked via GitHub API)
options.whatItDoes: Full open-source conferencing product. The parts that matter for our lane are its GUEST FLOW, which is the closest production analogue to Mama Fọláké in Ibadan: a URL opens in mobile Chrome with no account and no install; a 'prejoin' screen shows your own camera preview, a name field, and mic/camera toggles BEFORE you are visible to anyone; a 'lobby/knocking' mode holds the guest until a member admits them; ~90 language locales including a low-bandwidth 'audio only' mode toggle. It is worth reading its prejoin + lobby components as a spec for our own guest screen even if we never ship its code.

That is a second always-on stack on the Oracle arm64 box alongside Pipecat — realistically too much. Embedding the hosted meet.jit.si in an iframe is NO LONGER PERMITTED; embedding now requires 8x8 JaaS.
options.fitsUs: As a CODE dependency: poor. As a DESIGN reference for the elderly-guest flow (c): excellent and free. Its prejoin/lobby/audio-only patterns transfer directly to a hand-built Wàfè guest page.

options.risks: JaaS pricing is per MONTHLY ACTIVE USER, which for a marketplace family product scales exactly the wrong way — one 5-person family = 5 MAU, so ~5 families exhausts the free tier and ~60 families hits $99/mo. Self-hosting adds a JVM service and a second failure mode on the one VM. Treat as reference, not dependency.

options.name: livekit/components-js (@livekit/components-react)
options.maintained: Yes — repo pushed 2 Sep 2026; npm @livekit/components-react 2.9.24 published 11 Aug 2026
options.whatItDoes: Restylable React building blocks for a call UI: `<PreJoin>` (camera preview + device picker + permission prompt before joining — the exact 'is my camera on?' reassurance an older guest needs), `<RoomAudioRenderer>`, participant tiles, `useTracks`, connection-quality indicators, and a `<StartAudio>` gate for browsers that block autoplay audio. Headless enough that we can put warm Wàfè styling and 64px targets on it rather than fighting a corporate default skin.

For a family app the common case is 1:1, which does not need an SFU at all; components-react is most justified when Ifeoluwa + Oluwafemi + Mama Fọláké + Pastor Dayo are in one call.

A 20-minute 2-person video call ≈ 40 participant-minutes and ≈150MB, so ≈$0.04. Cheap per call, but the free 5,000 minutes is only ~125 such calls per MONTH ACROSS ALL TENANTS.

Self-hosting moves the cost to Oracle egress, which is capped-free at 10TB/mo but is now OUR bandwidth bill and OUR outage. options.name: katspaugh/wavesurfer.js
options.maintained: Yes — 7.12.11 published 17 Jul 2026; repo pushed 3 Sep 2026
options.whatItDoes: Audio waveform rendering and playback with a Record plugin (MediaRecorder wrapper) and playback-rate control. This is the concrete building block for VOICE NOTES — the single highest-value ritual for this product, because a voice note works for a five-year-old who cannot type, for a grandmother on a variable connection, and asynchronously across the UK/Nigeria time gap.

options.name: adobe/react-spectrum (react-aria / react-aria-components)
options.maintained: Yes — pushed 5 Sep 2026, very active
options.whatItDoes: Unstyled, rigorously accessible React primitives — dialogs with correct focus trapping, buttons with proper press handling on touch, listboxes, and (critically for us) hooks that handle screen-reader announcements and reduced-motion. The incoming-call modal, the 'admit this guest?' prompt and the contact picker are all patterns that are trivially easy to build inaccessibly by hand.
options.serverNeeded: None.
options.fitsUs: Very good — unstyled means it does not fight Tailwind v4 or the warm visual direction, and it is the standard way to satisfy requirement (d) without hand-writing ARIA. Import only the hooks used; it is tree-shakeable.
options.cost: Free, Apache-2.0.
options.risks: Large surface area and a learning curve; easy to over-adopt. Take react-aria hooks or react-aria-components selectively, not the Spectrum design system (which is a corporate look and would undo the warmth requirement).

options.name: WebAudio/web-speech-api (the browser SpeechRecognition API itself)
options.license: W3C incubation document repo (spec source, not a library) — the API ships in browsers, nothing to license
options.maintained: Yes — active incubation in the Web Audio Community Group; the on-device explainer lives in /explainers
options.whatItDoes: Free, zero-infrastructure live CAPTIONS and read-aloud. SpeechRecognition gives continuous interim transcripts we can render as captions during a call or auto-transcribe a voice note; SpeechSynthesis reads a message aloud for Ayo (5, pre-literate) or for Mama Fọláké if her eyes are tired. Chrome 139+ (Aug 2025) added a `processLocally` flag plus availability/install methods so recognition runs ON DEVICE.
options.serverNeeded: None whatsoever. This is the only captioning route that adds no cost and no service.
options.fitsUs: Best available fit for requirement (d) on our constraints, WITH one hard caveat below. Precedent is strong: FaceTime Live Captions (iOS 16+) are on-device and free, Google Meet captions are free and built in — captions are now table stakes, not a premium feature.
options.cost: Free.
options.risks: THE PRIVACY CAVEAT IS SERIOUS: `processLocally` defaults to FALSE, and in that default mode Chrome streams the audio to Google's servers for recognition. Shipping default-mode captions in a children's family app would mean silently sending a five-year-old's voice to a third party — unacceptable, and probably a UK GDPR/Children's Code problem. Rule: call `availableOnDevice()`, request on-device only, and if on-device is unavailable, offer captions OFF rather than falling back to cloud. Support is also uneven — Chromium and Safari (webkit-prefixed) yes, Firefox behind a flag; I could NOT verify whether on-device mode is available on Chrome for Android specifically, which is the device Mama Fọláké will actually use. Treat captions as progressive enhancement.

options.name: huggingface/transformers.js (Whisper in the browser)
options.maintained: Yes — pushed 7 Sep 2026, extremely active
options.whatItDoes: Runs Whisper ASR entirely client-side via ONNX Runtime/WebGPU. The privacy-clean way to caption a call or auto-transcribe a voice note with no audio leaving the device and no per-minute bill. Reference app: xenova/whisper-web (MIT, 3,341 stars) — but note that demo repo has not been pushed since Oct 2024.
options.serverNeeded: None at runtime, but the MODEL must be served — whisper-tiny/base quantised is roughly 40–80MB, and we would host it on Vercel or Supabase Storage and it must be added to the CSP.
options.fitsUs: Philosophically ideal, practically doubtful for our actual users. A 40–80MB model download over a Nigerian mobile connection before Grandma can see a caption is a non-starter, and low-end Android without WebGPU falls back to WASM where real-time transcription is unlikely.
options.cost: Free software; bandwidth cost of the model download, once per device if cached.
options.risks: I have NOT benchmarked this on a low-end Android, and I would not claim it works there. Whisper's accuracy on Nigerian-accented English and on Yorùbá code-switching — which is exactly what a call with Mama Fọláké contains — is materially worse than on US English; captions that mangle a grandmother's speech are worse than no captions. Suitable at most for OPTIONAL transcription of an already-recorded voice note on a good connection, not for live calls.

options.name: ccoreilly/vosk-browser
options.license: Apache-2.0 (wrapper); the Vosk MODELS carry their own licences — check each one
options.maintained: Marginal — last push 7 Dec 2025, single-maintainer project
options.whatItDoes: Kaldi/Vosk speech recognition compiled to WASM, running fully offline in a web worker. Small models (~50MB, some ~15MB) make it lighter than Whisper for on-device transcription.
options.serverNeeded: None; models served as static assets.
options.fitsUs: A fallback if we want offline transcription without Whisper's weight. Still a large download and still weak on our users' accents.
options.cost: Free.
options.risks: Single-maintainer, quiet for ~9 months, small community — a dependency I would not put on the critical path of a paid product. Model licences vary and must be checked individually before shipping. Accuracy on accented English is poor. Listed for completeness; I would not ship it.

options.name: Donaldcwl/browser-image-compression
options.maintained: STALE — last npm publish 2.0.2 on 6 Mar 2023 (3.5 years ago)
options.whatItDoes: Client-side image downscaling/compression in a web worker before upload. This matters more than it sounds: 'share a photo to the family album' is one of the core rituals, and a modern phone camera produces 4–8MB JPEGs. Uploading that from Croydon and then downloading it in Ibadan is a real, chargeable cost to Mama Fọláké.
options.serverNeeded: None — compress in the browser, upload to Supabase Storage.
options.fitsUs: Good, but consider doing it in ~40 lines with canvas + createImageBitmap rather than taking a three-year-old dependency.
options.cost: Free.
options.risks: Unmaintained for 3.5 years. The functionality is stable and small enough to vendor or reimplement; that is what I would do rather than depend on it. Whichever way, DO compress — see the data-cost note.

options.name: daily-co/daily-js (representing the per-minute SaaS category)
options.license: BSD-2-Clause (client SDK only — the SERVICE is proprietary and metered)
options.maintained: Yes — pushed 3 Sep 2026
options.whatItDoes: The easiest possible path: a prebuilt, already-accessible call UI you drop into a static SPA in an afternoon, plus managed TURN, so nothing new runs on our VM. GetStream/stream-video-js (124 stars, NOASSERTION licence, active) is the same shape.
options.serverNeeded: None of ours — that is the entire pitch.
options.fitsUs: Fits the STACK perfectly and fits the BUDGET badly. Worth naming honestly as the fastest route to a working demo.
options.cost: Metered per participant-minute. I did NOT verify Daily's current published rates, so I am not quoting a number — but the model is per-participant-minute, which is the model the brief specifically identifies as a serious problem.
options.risks: This is the exact 'per-minute SaaS bill that scales with usage' the brief rules out: a marketplace product where every family calling every Sunday turns straight into a variable bill against a fixed subscription price. Also a third-party origin in the CSP and a third party in the media path for children's calls — a disclosure and Children's Code question, not just a cost one. Recommend only as a time-boxed fallback if self-hosted WebRTC slips.

options.name: CommE2E/comm
options.maintained: Yes but small — pushed 25 Jul 2026
options.whatItDoes: An end-to-end-encrypted messaging app explicitly built around small private communities rather than public social graphs, with a per-community keyserver. Interesting as a product reference for 'a closed space with strong per-thread permissions', which is our shape.
options.serverNeeded: A keyserver per community — i.e. per family. Completely incompatible with our constraints.
options.fitsUs: Reference only, and a weak one.
options.cost: Free software; per-family server hosting is the model, which we cannot operate.
options.risks: Small project, small community, unusual architecture. Listed for honesty because it came up in the search; I would not build on it.

recommendation:
BUILD THE TOGETHER CAPABILITY OURSELVES AT THE PRODUCT LAYER, AND BUY NOTHING PER-MINUTE.

Nothing I found is a "family chat + calling" component we can install. Every open-source option is either infrastructure (Jitsi, Element Call, Nextcloud Talk — all needing services we cannot honestly operate on one shared Oracle VM) or a per-minute SaaS (Daily, Stream, LiveKit Cloud past its free tier), and the free tiers all bite at roughly 25–40 active families, which is not a business. What IS reusable is small, boring and free: wavesurfer.js for voice notes, react-aria for accessible dialogs, the browser's own SpeechRecognition (on-device mode only) for captions, and Jitsi's prejoin/lobby flow read as a design spec rather than imported as code.

So the recommendation is a product one, in this order:

1) SHIP ASYNC BEFORE LIVE. The single most important finding in this research is that the warmest family-communication product of the last decade — Marco Polo — is not a calling app at all. It is asynchronous video/voice messaging, and users describe it as helping people feel close "without the pressure of live calls", working around busy schedules AND connectivity issues. That is precisely the Croydon↔Ibadan problem: a five-hour-a-day overlap of good moods, a variable connection, and a grandmother who should not have to be free at 14:00. A voice note in the family thread needs zero new infrastructure (MediaRecorder → Supabase Storage → a Postgres row → Realtime), works on any phone, costs ~180KB per minute, and is usable by both Ayo at 5 and Mama Fọláké at 68. Build this first. It is the ritual; live calling is the occasion.

2) MAKE THE CONTACT GRAPH A DATABASE FACT, NOT A UI STATE. The definitive cautionary tale is Messenger Kids' July 2019 flaw: children were pulled into GROUP chats containing friends-of-friends their parents had never approved — the app failing at its only job, discovered 12 June, fixed the next day, parents told only on 15 July. The failure was architectural: per-contact approval enforced at the one-to-one layer, then bypassed by group membership. For Wàfè: every call room and every thread must have an explicit membership row, and RLS must evaluate "may this child be in a room with this person" on the ROOM, on every join, per participant — never trust the client, never let an invite from a sibling widen a child's graph. A guest link must resolve to a single-use, single-room, expiring token bound to one invited person, not a bearer URL that grants entry to whoever holds it. Design the schema so "who Dami may talk to" is answerable by one SQL query.

3) SUPERVISION MUST BE DISCLOSED TO THE CHILD, IN THE CHILD'S WORDS. Messenger Kids does the honest version and we should copy it outright: it shows children a kid-written version of the privacy policy stating that "parents can see and download messages their children send and receive like texts, photos and videos" and can "see who you talk to most", uses illustrations to explain it, and — the best detail — NOTIFIES THE CHILD IN-APP WHEN A PARENT REQUESTS THEIR DATA. The research backs this: Ghosh & Wisniewski's CHI 2018 "Safety vs. Surveillance", built from children's own reviews of parental-control apps, found heavy-handed monitoring that ignores teens' privacy and autonomy is what makes these apps disliked and underused. Concrete Wàfè rules: (a) age-tiered by default — a 5- and 9-year-old's threads are parent-visible, a 15-year-old's are NOT read by default, with parents seeing only who and when, not what; (b) an always-visible badge in the child's thread header ("Mum and Dad can read this") rather than a buried policy; (c) every parental read of a child's content writes an audit row and pings the child. Say plainly in the marketing copy that Wàfè does not offer covert monitoring. That is a differentiator, not a limitation.

4) FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD: PHOTOS, NOT NAMES, AND A SHARED THING TO DO. The one-tap "call Grandma" tile with a face photo, in a grid of only parent-approved people, is table stakes (Kinzoo builds its whole product on parent-approved contacts). The deeper finding is what happens AFTER the call connects. Myers et al., "Baby FaceTime: can toddlers learn from online video chat?" (Developmental Science, 2017) showed that live, socially CONTINGENT video chat — unlike recorded video — produced children who recognised and preferred their partner a week later and learned more; contingency is the active ingredient, not the video. But a talking head does not hold a five-year-old, which is why every serious attempt added a shared activity: Portal's Story Time (AR-illustrated books read together over the call) and Amazon Glow's projected shared play; Kinzoo Together's differentiator today is games, stories and activities INSIDE the video call. And DIS 2026 (Geiskkovitch, Neustaedter, Lei & Forghani, "Exploring the Needs of Preschool-aged Children, Parents, and Grandparents for Communicating Over Distance") names the design tensions directly: children's independence versus parental control, and the need for CHILD-LED BURSTS of interaction rather than scheduled sit-downs. So: give Ayo a tile with Mama Fọláké's face, let him initiate whenever (parent-approved contact, so no gate), and put one shared thing on the screen — a photo from the family album they both scroll, a story, a drawing canvas. Cheapest credible v1: "look at this together", where both ends see the same album photo and either can swipe.

5) FOR MAMA FỌLÁKÉ: A LINK, A LOBBY, AND AUDIO FIRST. FaceTime's web links are the pattern to copy — anyone on Android or Windows joins from a browser with no app and no account; they enter a name, grant mic/camera, and then WAIT FOR THE HOST TO ADMIT THEM. That last step is both the safety mechanism and the warmth mechanism, and it costs nothing. Then be honest about data: WhatsApp video runs ~5MB/min (~300MB/hour, ~480MB/hour HD) against ~0.3–0.5MB/min for voice; 1GB in Nigeria is around ₦500. A 30-minute video call spends roughly ₦75 of Mama Fọláké's own money; the same call in audio spends about ₦5. Therefore: default the guest to AUDIO with a large, obvious "turn on video" button; show an honest data estimate before joining; degrade to audio automatically on packet loss and SAY SO ("video paused to save your data") rather than freezing silently. Interface per the older-adult usability literature (NN/g and the AHP-prioritised barrier study: small fonts, small buttons and low contrast rank as the top barrier, complex interfaces second): one screen, ≤3 controls, WCAG 2.2 AAA target size 44×44 CSS px minimum (2.5.5) rather than the 24×24 AA floor (2.5.8) — I would go 64px — a permanently visible red HANG UP that is never hidden behind a hover or an auto-hiding toolbar, and no login, no password, no account.

6) ACCESSIBILITY: CAPTIONS ARE TABLE STAKES AND MUST BE ON-DEVICE. FaceTime Live Captions (iOS 16+) run on the device's own ASR with no cloud, and Google Meet gives captions free; users now expect them. Use the browser SpeechRecognition API with `processLocally: true` and check `availableOnDevice()` first — and if on-device is unavailable, offer NO captions rather than the default cloud path, which silently streams audio to Google. Pair with: SpeechSynthesis read-aloud on every message (Ayo cannot read; Mama Fọláké may not want to), full `prefers-reduced-motion` support, live regions announcing "Tobi joined", captions on voice notes as text, and — a small thing that matters enormously — a language/Yorùbá-name pronunciation that is correct, because a family app that mangles Ifeoluwa and Fọláké is not warm.

7) TIE CALLS TO THE CALENDAR, WHICH IS THE THING WÀFÈ ALREADY HAS. "Video call with Mama Fọláké at 14:00" should render as a JOIN button in the event, fire a reminder to both households at T-10 in each person's own timezone (Ibadan is UTC+1, and the WAT/BST offset shifts twice a year — get this right), and if the call is missed, offer "send her a voice note instead" in the same tap. This is the integration no competitor can copy, because Cozi has the family calendar but is an organiser (calendar, lists, meals, journal, a light message feature) with no calling, while Marco Polo has the warmth but no family operating system. Wàfè's actual differentiator is that the ritual and the schedule live in one place.

8) WHAT THE POST-MORTEMS TEACH: DON'T SELL HARDWARE, AND DON'T BE CREEPY. Portal was technically good and died anyway — launched weeks after Cambridge Analytica, asking families to put a Facebook camera in the living room; under 1% of the smart-display market, ~600k units in 2020, and discontinued for consumers in 2022. Glow was $300, invitation-only, needed a flat surface and a good connection, had ~500 reviews, and was killed 12 months in as a pandemic-shaped product in a reopened world. Both lessons point the same way for us: no device, no new hardware, run in the browser the family already has; and lead with the privacy architecture (closed space, no strangers, no ads, no algorithmic feed, disclosed supervision) because in this category trust is the product. Also note Marco Polo's more recent user backlash over price rises and paywalling previously-free features — async video is expensive to STORE, so set retention and quality policy at design time, not after the storage bill arrives.

CONCRETE FIRST SLICE (product order, not build order): family thread with text + voice notes + photo-to-album + six large reactions → per-person contact tiles with photos, membership enforced in RLS → 1:1 audio call, audio-first, with a guest link that lands on a prejoin screen and a host admit step → video toggle with an honest data warning → on-device captions as progressive enhancement → calendar join buttons → shared-photo "look at this together" during a call. Group calling last, since it is the only part that genuinely needs an SFU.
notes:
SCOPE AND HONESTY

My lane was the product side, but the output schema wanted repositories, so the options list is the set of concrete, verified building blocks that implement the product patterns. Every star count, licence, and last-commit/last-publish date above was checked directly against the GitHub API or the npm registry on 7 Sep 2026, not recalled. Two I could not verify by API (rate limit) I checked by fetching the repo page and the npm registry instead — browser-image-compression (1.7k stars, MIT, last publish 2.0.2 on 6 Mar 2023) and the web-speech-api spec repo (187 stars, W3C incubation, no library licence because there is no library).

WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY, AND WILL NOT GUESS
- Daily's and Stream's current per-minute rates. I know the model is per-participant-minute; I did not read their pricing pages, so I quote no figures.
- Whether Chrome for Android supports the Web Speech API's on-device `processLocally` mode. Chrome 139 (desktop, Aug 2025) added it. Android is the device that actually matters for Mama Fọláké and I could not confirm it. Captions must therefore be built as progressive enhancement with a clean "not available on this device" state — not as a promised feature.
- Whisper/transformers.js real-world performance on a low-end Android over a Nigerian connection. I would expect the 40–80MB model download alone to disqualify it there, but I have not benchmarked it and am not claiming a number.
- The DIS 2026 preprint's full text — ACM DL returned 403. I have the title, the four authors (Geiskkovitch, Neustaedter, Lei, Forghani), the venue and the reported themes from the abstract-level summary, not the full findings.
- Kinzoo's and Zoog's current commercial status. Both are small companies in a category with a high death rate (see Portal, Glow); I would not assume either is still trading in a year, which is another argument for building rather than integrating.

THINGS THAT WOULD BITE US, RANKED
1. Per-MAU and per-minute pricing. 8x8 JaaS is free to 25 monthly active users then $99/mo to 300 — one five-person family is five MAU, so the free tier holds about five families. LiveKit Cloud's free 5,000 WebRTC participant-minutes is about 125 twenty-minute two-person calls PER MONTH ACROSS ALL TENANTS. Both are demo-sized. Any option whose bill is a function of family usage is structurally wrong for a marketplace product with a fixed subscription price.
2. AGPL. Element Call and Nextcloud Talk are both AGPL-3.0. For a network-served commercial product this is a copyleft exposure — read them, never copy them.
3. The Web Speech API default. `processLocally` defaults to false, and in that mode Chrome sends audio to Google. Shipping default-mode captions in a children's app would mean quietly transmitting a five-year-old's voice to a third party. This is a UK Children's Code / GDPR issue, not merely a preference, and it is easy to ship by accident because the API "just works" in the wrong mode.
4. Stale dependencies on the critical path: browser-image-compression (3.5 years), emoji-mart (~2 years), whisper-web demo (~2 years), chatscope (~16 months, and no post-React-19 release). Each is individually small enough to vendor or reimplement; none should be a load-bearing dependency in a paid product.
5. TURN. Not my lane, but it touches the product: relay is genuinely required on many mobile/symmetric-NAT paths, especially Nigerian carriers, and relayed video is roughly 300MB/hour of OUR bandwidth per stream if we run our own coturn. Oracle's free egress allowance is large but finite, and "the call worked in testing but relays in Lagos" is exactly the failure the plumbing lane needs to cost honestly. The product-side mitigation is the same either way: default to audio, which is ~1/10th the bytes.

ONE UNCOMFORTABLE PRODUCT OBSERVATION
The brief says WhatsApp is one of the disconnected tools Wàfè replaces. Every product I looked at that tried to replace WhatsApp for family video specifically — Portal, Glow — is dead, and the survivors (Marco Polo, Kinzoo) won by doing something WhatsApp does NOT do rather than doing calling better. Wàfè should not try to beat WhatsApp at live video quality; it cannot and does not need to. It should win on the things WhatsApp structurally cannot do: a closed, parent-curated contact graph with honest disclosure; calls that are part of the family's schedule and album rather than a separate app; and asynchronous voice that survives a five-hour time gap and a bad connection. If a family ends up doing their long Sunday video call on WhatsApp and everything else in Wàfè, that is a perfectly good outcome for v1 — and a deep-link "call her on WhatsApp" button is a more honest feature than a worse video call.
